prompt: Which of these is a tactical question, in the lesson's sense?
hint: Weeks and months, managers, resources to move.

choices.text: Which customer's delivery window closes in the next hour?
choices.why: Minutes and one order: that is operational, lesson 14.

choices.text: Should Varanda open its first stores outside Minas Gerais over the next five years?
choices.why: Years and the owners: that is strategic, lesson 16.

choices.text: Why did the site stop taking payments at 14:00 today?
choices.why: An incident today is operational, and its cause is a diagnosis for whoever runs the site.

choices.text: Which channels bought orders at the planned cost?
choices.why: Right: a month of data, a manager, and budget to move between channels.

prompt: Why does every number on a tactical screen sit beside both the budget and the same month last year?
hint: Each comparison is only as good as something.

choices.text: The budget tests the plan and last year carries the season
choices.why: Right: a budget is only as good as the plan, and last year only fair if the months are alike.

choices.text: Auditors require the two comparisons on any management report
choices.why: The lesson gives a reason about what each comparison catches, not a rule from outside.

choices.text: The two together cancel out the effect of a campaign that moved
choices.why: Neither cancels it; the footnote and the two-month comparison deal with the moved campaign.

choices.text: Last year is the target, and the budget is a forecast
choices.why: It is the other way round: the budget is the plan, and last year is history.

prompt: Halfway through November, a weekly check compares orders so far with half of the month's target. Why does the lesson call that a poor yardstick?
hint: When did the campaign run?

choices.text: Orders are final once the month closes, so a check before the close means little
choices.why: The lesson keeps the weekly check; the problem is the yardstick, not checking early.

choices.text: The campaign ran from the 3rd to the 13th, so many orders land early
choices.why: Right: the target arrives unevenly, and the expected part by a date has to follow the month's shape.

choices.text: Half of a target is a percentage of a percentage
choices.why: Half of 4,800 orders is 2,400 orders; nothing is wrong with the arithmetic.

choices.text: Weekly checks belong to operational BI
choices.why: A week inside a monthly plan is tactical; operational works in minutes.

prompt: The monthly review uses the ___ figures, the ones finance reports after the books are done, not a count taken on the first day of the next month.
hint: Otávio does it on the fifth working day.

prompt: The online shop sold R$ 1,370 thousand in October 2024 and R$ 1,660 thousand in November 2024; in 2025, R$ 1,080 thousand and R$ 2,060 thousand. By how many percent did the two months together grow? One decimal.
hint: Add each year's two months before comparing.

prompt: In November, social ads cost R$ 84 thousand and brought 1,090 orders. What did each order cost, in reais, to one decimal?
hint: Thousands of reais times 1,000, divided by orders.

prompt: All of November's media spend divided by all of November's orders gives R$ 36.7 an order; divided by the orders from paid channels, R$ 48.7. Why is the first figure the flattering one?
hint: Look at what the denominator contains.

choices.text: It leaves out email, the cheapest channel
choices.why: Email is in both; leaving it out would raise the figure, not lower it.

choices.text: It was computed before the month closed, when cancelled orders were still in
choices.why: Both use the closed month; the difference is which orders are counted.

choices.text: Its denominator counts 1,270 organic and direct orders that no media paid for
choices.why: Right: a hidden denominator, which flatters the media by the size of those orders.

choices.text: It divides thousands of reais by orders without converting the unit first, which shrinks the result
choices.why: Both figures are in reais per order; the unit is handled the same way in each.

prompt: The agency's report says social ads had their best month by cost per visit. Why does Renata's review judge channels by cost per order instead?
hint: What is Varanda paying for?

choices.text: Cost per visit cannot be computed for email, so the screen needs one measure that works across the channels
choices.why: Visits are counted for every channel, email included; that is not the reason.

choices.text: Cost per order is what finance reports in the closed month
choices.why: Finance closes the books; the choice of measure follows what the business pays for.

choices.text: Orders change less from month to month, so the trend is easier to read
choices.why: Stability is not the argument; the argument is what the measure counts.

choices.text: A visit is what the agency sells; an order is what Varanda wants
choices.why: Right: lesson 12's vanity-metric test, turned into a column.

prompt: Which of these belong on the screen of Renata's monthly review? Choose all that apply.
hint: What the meeting has to answer, and no more.

choices.text: Online sales against the budget and against November 2024
choices.why: Right: a number beside the two numbers it is judged against.

choices.text: Every ad's clicks for the month
choices.why: That detail lives one step behind the screen, for the analyst after the meeting.

choices.text: A footnote saying the yearly campaign moved into November
choices.why: Right: it stops a moved campaign from passing for growth.

choices.text: Cost per order by channel, against each channel's target
choices.why: Right: the column the meeting decides on.

choices.text: A chart of visits day by day
choices.why: It answers no question the meeting has to decide; it turns the review into a reading.

prompt: Free-delivery offers had a budget of R$ 40 thousand and cost R$ 52 thousand. What is the variance as a percentage of the budget?
hint: (actual − budget) ÷ budget × 100.

prompt: A variance is the actual figure minus the ___.
hint: What was planned.

prompt: Match each November line with how the review reads it.
hint: The sign, the kind of line, the reason, the size.

pairs.right: Unfavourable, and big enough to discuss
Favourable on paper; the shoot moved to December
Favourable, and too small to discuss

prompt: Content production came in R$ 8 thousand under budget and the sheet marks it F. Why does the review not count it as a saving?
hint: Where did the money go?

choices.text: The IF formula marks a cost below budget as F without looking at what kind of line it is
choices.why: The formula checks the kind of line first; for this cost line its F is correct arithmetic.

choices.text: The shoot slipped into December, which will carry the R$ 8 thousand
choices.why: Right: a timing variance moves between months; a real one does not come back.

choices.text: Variances under 30% are noise
choices.why: The lesson's threshold is R$ 5 thousand and 10%, and this line passes both.

choices.text: Content is a revenue line, so below budget is bad
choices.why: It is a cost line; the question is whether the money was saved or only moved.

prompt: Free-delivery offers ran R$ 12 thousand over budget in a month with 5,150 orders instead of the 4,800 planned. What does dividing the cost by orders add?
hint: Volume, or something else as well?

choices.text: It shows R$ 10.10 an order against R$ 8.33 planned, so more than volume moved
choices.why: Right: part followed the extra orders, and part is a larger share of customers using the offer.

choices.text: It proves the whole overrun came from the extra 350 orders
choices.why: If volume were all of it, the cost per order would match the plan, and it does not.

choices.text: It turns the U into an F, because the cost per order is what the budget is measured against
choices.why: The budget is in reais for the month; dividing explains the variance without changing its verdict.

choices.text: Nothing, since the percentage already says 30%
choices.why: The percentage says how much; it cannot separate volume from the share using the offer.

prompt: Put the month of Renata's review in order, from the close of the books to the end of the meeting.
hint: The meeting opens with promises, not with numbers.
items: Lívia drafts the findings with Renata from the screen
The meeting checks last month's actions
The meeting discusses at most three findings
Each action gets an owner, a date and a measure
trap: Opening with the new numbers feels natural, and it lets last month's actions expire without anybody asking.

prompt: Paid search delivered orders at R$ 51.6 in November. Why is moving R$ 15 thousand into it written as a test and not a transfer?
hint: Average cost, and the cost of the next order.

choices.text: The budget stays fixed until Otávio closes December, and money moves after that
choices.why: Money moves between channels inside a month; the closing date is not the obstacle.

choices.text: Search is above its target, so it needs proof first
choices.why: Search came in under its target of R$ 55.

choices.text: R$ 51.6 is the average so far; the next R$ 15 thousand buys weaker searches
choices.why: Right: nobody knows what the extra orders will cost, so the action is something to measure.

choices.text: The agency has to approve a move of budget between the channels it runs for Varanda
choices.why: The lesson mentions no such approval; the reason is in the numbers.

prompt: What is wrong with a monthly review that reads each number aloud and ends on time?
hint: What changes next month?

choices.text: It takes too long, because reading every number aloud costs the managers an hour of their month
choices.why: It ends on time; the cost is what it fails to produce.

choices.text: The numbers are not closed yet when it happens
choices.why: The scenario says nothing about the close; the problem is what the meeting does with the numbers.

choices.text: It decides nothing
choices.why: Right: no finding becomes an action, so next month's screen is read aloud the same way.

choices.text: Numbers should be sent by email and not shown on a screen
choices.why: The format is not the problem; a meeting with a screen can decide plenty.

prompt: Which of these is written the way the lesson's action list asks?
hint: What, who, by when, and how we will know.

choices.text: Improve social ads.
choices.why: No owner, no date, no measure: it is a wish.

choices.text: The team will look into social ads and report back soon.
choices.why: "The team" and "soon" are nobody and never.

choices.text: Stop the two weakest ad sets; paid-media analyst; by 10 Dec; December's cost per order
choices.why: Right: an action, an owner, a date and the number that will show whether it worked.

choices.text: Renata to decide about social ads at some point.
choices.why: An owner without a date or a measure is never late, so it is never done.

prompt: In January, the first finding of Caio's review is that the Betim store's overtime ran 25% over budget in December. Before calling it a problem, what does this lesson ask first?
hint: Two of the three things a variance does not tell you.

choices.text: Whether the other eight stores ran over by the same amount
choices.why: A useful comparison later, but it does not say whether the overrun was timing or a cost of success.

choices.text: Whether it is timing or real, and what the extra hours bought
choices.why: Right: an unfavourable line can be the cost of a success, and a variance alone cannot tell.

choices.text: Whether 25% is above the review's threshold of 30% for any line
choices.why: The lesson's threshold is R$ 5 thousand and 10%; 30% was one line's variance.

choices.text: Who approved the overtime, so that the cost can be charged back to the people involved
choices.why: The review looks for what the number means and what to do next, not someone to bill.

prompt: Helena sees November's online sales 24.1% above November 2024 and proposes raising the 2026 online target by the same amount. What should Lívia show her?
hint: Lesson 7 and the footnote.

choices.text: That November also beat its budget by 8.4%, which supports a higher target
choices.why: Beating the budget in one month that borrowed a campaign from October supports nothing about a year.

choices.text: That social ads cost more than their target, so growth will slow
choices.why: True of social ads, but it does not answer why November grew 24.1%.

choices.text: That the campaign moved from October, and the two months together grew 3.6%
choices.why: Right: the 24.1% is the calendar; 3.6% is the comparable growth.

choices.text: That a year's target is not built from one month
choices.why: Sound in general, but it leaves her believing the 24.1%, which is the real problem.

prompt: Match each comparison with what it tells a tactical review.
hint: One of them tells a retailer very little.

pairs.left: Against the same month last year
pairs.right: How the business moved, with the season taken into account
Little for a retailer: December beats November every year

pairs.left: Month so far against the part of the target due by now
pairs.right: An early warning, if the target follows the month's shape
